newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection begins in Jacksonville case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection begins in Jacksonville case.

text.p: The attorney who dealt cigarette makers their worse courtroom defeat in 40 years sought another court victory Monday as jury selection began in the latest trial of a lawsuit against the tobacco industry.

In another Florida case, Philip Morris Cos. Inc. Chief Executive Officer Geoffrey Bible, was ordered by a Miami court to answer pretrial questions from attorneys suing tobacco companies on behalf of non-smoking flight attendants who say they were injured by secondhand smoke.

The state jury being picked in Jacksonville is slated to hear the trial of a lawsuit against the R.J. Reynolds tobacco company by the family of Jean Connor, whose 1995 death of cancer at age 49 they blame on smoking. The family is seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages.

The case is the first tobacco trial for plaintiff's attorney Norwood "Woody" Wilner since August, when he won a landmark $750,000 verdict against B.A.T Industries' Brown & Williamson unit. Brown & Williamson has appealed the award in favour of a lifelong smoker with lung cancer.
In the current trial, Wilner said he would charge that Reynolds, America's second-largest cigarette maker, deceived the public with misleading ads.
Winston-Salem, N.C.-based Reynolds' attorneys have contended that Connor made an informed decision to smoke.

Her sister, Dana Raulerson -- the plaintiff on behalf of Connor's estate and her three children -- was in court for the beginning of the closely watched case Monday, as were journalists and tobacco industry analysts from New York.

The pool of 53 potential jurors was given a list of 50 questions, including whether they had ever told anyone to stop smoking, had strong feelings about cigarette companies, thought the government should ban the sale of cigarettes or had a friend or family member die of lung cancer.
Six jurors and three alternates were to be selected for the case, which Judge Bernard Nachman said would probably last two to three weeks.
Jury selection was expected to take several days, and opening statements were expected to begin later this week.

Wilner's August victory hurt tobacco companies on Wall Street and emboldened anti-tobacco activists, who have filed hundreds of individual lawsuits. State governments also have sued the industry, seeking $30 billion in Medicaid costs. The industry is also under a regulatory assualt by Washington.
The stock of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., R.J. Reynolds' parent, climbed 62.5 cents Monday to $31.125 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

In the Miami flight attendants' case, Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye ruled in favour of Stanley Rosenblatt, an attorney for one of the estimated 60,000 plaintiffs. Rosenblatt said he needed to question CEO Bible because he is a leading Philip Morris spokesman on tobacco policy matters.

But an attorney for New York-based Philip Morris said Kaye's ruling would probably be challenged in a New York court and that Bible would probably not be available for questioning until early next month.
Attorneys representing Philip Morris said in a hearing that Bible was head of the Philip Morris parent organisation and had no direct responsibilities in cigarette manufacturing.
Rosenblatt is slated to question the heads of cigarette units of Philip Morris and other companies in New York next week.
Kaye also ordered that several of the questions and answers resulting from the pretrial sessions in New York be kept secret.
A Philip Morris attorney, David Hardy, said some of the questioning next week would be based on privileged industry documents and that the answers should be kept secret.
The trial is scheduled to begin June 2.
Philip Morris stock dipped 12.5 cents to $113.25 in consolidated trading on the NYSE.
